short: A biblical name for the place of final punishment.
note: A name derived from the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem, used in the New Testament for the place of final punishment. Mark 9 associates it with unquenchable fire.

short: The angel who guides and heals in Tobit.
note: The angel who accompanies Tobiah and helps restore Tobit’s sight. In Tobit 12 he identifies himself as one of the seven angels who stand before God.

short: An ancient town beside an oracle of the dead.
note: An ancient town in Epirus associated with the Nekromanteion of Acheron, where worshippers sought communication with the dead.

sources.label: Hellenic Ministry of Culture: Nekromanteion of Acheron

short: A Greek river associated with the underworld.
note: A river in Epirus and, in Greek and Roman mythology, a river of the realm of the dead, crossed by the ferryman Charon.

short: The ancient oracle of Zeus in Epirus.
note: An ancient sanctuary and oracle of Zeus and Dione in northwestern Greece, famed for divination associated with its sacred oak.

sources.label: Theoi: ancient sources on Dione and Dodona

short: Lake Avernus, a classical entrance to the underworld.
note: The Italian name for Lake Avernus, a volcanic lake near Naples associated with the entrance to the underworld in Virgil’s Aeneid.

sources.label: Campi Flegrei archaeological park: Virgil’s places

short: Mary Shelley’s creator of an artificial human.
note: Victor Frankenstein, the scientist in Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818), who creates a living being and abandons it.

short: The warning over Dante’s gate of Hell.
note: Italian for abandon all hope, the opening of the gate’s final warning in Dante’s Inferno, canto III: those who enter must leave hope behind.
Formal language for washing the body.
A ring like the radiance painted around a sacred figure; a halo or similar surrounding ring.
Uprightness of character, especially reliable honesty and trustworthiness.
Quick to understand or perceive another person’s feelings or a situation.
